# Stewarding a pull request here
Read this before acting on a CI failure or a review comment.
It states only where this repository differs from the general rules; everything not named here is unchanged, and nothing here loosens a prohibition.
## S1 A red claim, closure or pin check is a bot's job, not yours
IF `fast` fails with `INHERITED CLAIMS`, `closures` prints `UNDER-SCOPED`, or `mutation` refuses unpinned sites, THEN wait for the autofix job's commit and push nothing.
The repairs already exist as jobs.
A branch that touches no fixture inherits the baseline's claim list through the merge, and the repair is to empty it — which the bot does, and which you must not do by hand.

**Read the job's summary line, not its tick.** The job reports its own status and goes red exactly when the repair did not happen: `autofix_repair_failed` in `tests/closure.py` decides that, and print
Green covers both "repaired, commit coming" and "nothing was owed", and the conclusion alone cannot tell them apart.
Once the job has gone red it has told you no commit is coming, and the rule against repairing it yourself stops applying.
EXAMPLE BAD: emptying the claim file and pushing while the job is still running.
GOOD: reading the summary, seeing `changed`, and waiting for it.
## S2 A conflicted pull request is not red — it cannot run
IF the pull request is `DIRTY`, THEN no workflow fired and there is no result to read.
Merge `origin/main` locally and push; the merge driver for the claim files runs only in a clone that installed it, and a runner is not one.
This happens without anyone touching your branch: a merge to the default branch that moves a claim file flips every open pull request at once.
Confirm a conflict is real before treating it as one:
git merge-tree --write-tree origin/main HEAD
Install the driver once per clone; a worktree shares its checkout's config.
python3 tests/env_drift.py --install-merge-driver
## S3 Key on the mode line, never the count
IF the scoped selection prints a mode line, THEN act on the mode.
Both modes can print zero, and they mean opposite things.
A push to the default branch prints no mode line at all, because the forced full run never calls the code that would.
## S4 Never move a version
IF your change would touch `VERSION`, the integration manifest version, or the release-notes heading, THEN stop.
Versions are assigned after the merge by `tools/release/stamp.py`, which refuses a branch that moved one.
## S5 Leave the claim files alone unless you are claiming
IF your branch moves no fixture, THEN both claim files stay byte-identical to the default branch.
A branch that does not touch them cannot conflict with another branch over them, and the guard that catches an inherited list is satisfied by an empty one.
## S6 Take no lease by hand for a gate run
IF a local run selects `tests/stress.py`, THEN let `tests/run.sh` take the gate lease; it does, around that run alone.
Holding it by hand is `.claude/rules/gate-scoping.md`'s; a `stress.py` run outside `run.sh` takes none, and `dev/audit/README.md` wraps it.
## S7 Merge, never rebase, and never force-push
IF you are updating a branch from the default branch, THEN merge.
A rebase invalidates the head a reviewer measured and every checkout of it.
## S8 A red check owes an answer in the body
IF your branch turned any required check red, THEN name it in the body and answer it: the cheaper detector, or that none exists.
The one required check is `gate`, red whenever a unit is, so answer the units `pr-contract` lists (`tests / closures`) and each `code-scanning alert <n> (<rule id>)`, not `gate`.
An unanswered one is a blocked verdict.
Naming a trigger is not the analysis.
`delivery-status` is not required.
PENDING a row is ordinary; only OVERDUE is a stopped batch.
Read its list, or `tests/delivery_status.py --emit`.
## S9 Never re-gate an unchanged head
IF a terminal result already exists at this head, THEN it is the result.
Re-run a job only under the narrow conditions the general rules allow, and never to see whether it comes out differently.
## S10 Create the commit, then write the body, then push, then confirm
IF a fix also needs the pull-request body corrected, THEN create the commit first, write the body against the SHA it already has, push last, and check the head's own checks afterwards.
`pr-contract` runs last in `ci.yml`, on `synchronize`, and reads the body as it stood at push time.
Push before correcting the body and the job measures the stale one.
Both orders leave exactly one failed run.
The difference is WHERE, and that is the whole reason for this order:
* push, then edit — the failure lands on the commit that is your head, and the pull request carries it while it is under review;
* edit, then push — the body edit fires an `edited` run against the head of that moment, which is the one you are abandoning, so the failure lands on a commit that is never the head again.
Measured here at two heads: an `edited` run failing on the outgoing commit within seconds of a `synchronize` run passing on the incoming one.
A commit's SHA is assigned when the commit is MADE, not when it is pushed -- a cherry-pick assigns it locally too -- so `## Head` can always be written before the push.
What cannot is writing it before the commit exists.
The race is detectable, not preventable, so confirm rather than assume: read the check runs on the head you just pushed, not on the pull request as a whole.
A failure on an earlier commit is expected and harmless; one on the head is not.
The same applies to a push you did not make.
An autofix commit (S1) is a `synchronize` event, and your body then names the head before the bot's commit.
`pr-contract` accepts it; fix `## Head` only if red.
EXAMPLE BAD: push, then update the body, then explain the red run on your head.
GOOD: commit, read the SHA, write the body, push, then read that head's checks.

## Identity — who authors, approves, runs and stamps (decision 0011)
Pull requests are authored by the `hpo-author` App via `tools/pr/app_push.sh` (never `push.sh`, never `tvofi`); `pr-contract` refuses any other author.
`hpo-approver` posts verdicts, approves non-code-owned PRs; only `@tvofi` reviews code-owned paths.
`hpo-runs` approves held CI runs; stamps push over the deploy key (`stamp.py --push --push-key`).
Retired `tvofi-seat-author` never writes.

The owner approves a change to any of it before **merging**, not drafting — so open the pull request and surface it.
Approval is the owner's approving GitHub review, which `main-protect-checks`'s code-owner rule requires (0009 step 6).
Every rewrite looks like a correction from the inside; if the honest description is *"this changes what a seat must do"*, it is policy however small the diff.

Filing is not neutral: an issue enters the Delivery-status table, needs a disposition, and is read by later seats as established fact — it propagates further than a wrong pull request, because nothing

# Security
Private vulnerability reporting is already enabled on this repository.
Do not open a public issue for a vulnerability.
Report it through GitHub's private advisory form:
https://github.com/tvofi/heatpump_optimizer/security/advisories/new
That is the Security tab, then Advisories, then Report a vulnerability.
Include the affected version (`VERSION` at the repository root), what happens, and enough to reproduce it.
Fixes ship in a release of the integration.
The supported line is the latest `v*` tag.

## The work, in order
audit → [design → design review, for an L or XL group] → fix → fix review → train → merge → record → stamp.
The order is the orchestrator's contract, `dev/governance/roles/orchestrator.md`, with the design step from `dev/governance/roles/designer.md` and `dev/governance/roles/design-review.md`.

**Audit: find, verify, judge.** One finder per scope of `dev/audit/config/scopes.json`, against a pinned baseline, under `dev/governance/roles/COMMON.md`: a finding carries a claim, evidence, a harnes

Evidence lands under `dev/audit/rounds/`, causes under `dev/audit/rca/`.

The design reviewer reads it at its handoff SHA, and only `Design review: approve <sha>`, read back, dispatches the fixer.
The approved note is the group's architect note.

**Fix review.** `dev/governance/roles/fix-review.md`: a fresh context in a detached worktree at the head SHA, using the finder's harness, never the fixer's.

# Posting a comment, and proving it landed
**Post an issue or pull-request comment by running the poster, and read back what landed.** The read-back is the obligation; the poster is how you get it without doing anything extra.

``` python3 tools/pr/gh_comment.py post --repo O/R --issue N --body-file F python3 tools/pr/gh_comment.py patch --repo O/R --comment I --body-file F python3 tools/pr/gh_comment.py verify --repo O/R --
`post` and `patch` write, then fetch the comment off the API and exit non-zero unless what is on the record is byte-identical to the file.
`verify` is the read-back on its own, for a comment written some other way — a client's own comment verb, or the mapping in `.claude/workflows/web-fragments.md` for a seat with no such binary.
Either route is fine.
Ending without a read-back is not.
## Why this prescribes rather than prohibits
The defect it replaces is a field flag whose two spellings differ by the case of one letter.

The wrong one sends the literal string `@FILE` as the body, exits 0, and returns a well-formed comment object carrying an id and a URL, so nothing between typing it and believing it worked carries a s
Four instances in one day.
Three were in seats whose dispatch carried a specific, correct, written warning naming that exact flag, and none of the three complied — **0 of 3**.
Across the same seats on the same day, the instruction *read your comment back* was complied with **4 of 4**.

The root-cause seat (#541 comment 5625671141) attributes the gap to what compliance leaves behind: a warning is discharged inside one seat's head, while a read-back prints a line some other seat can r
So "never write that flag" is the shape already measured at 0 of 3, and a fifth copy of it would be a fifth copy of the thing that did not work.
What is required here is the artifact instead: a posted comment with a read-back beside it.
Which flag you avoided is between you and your shell.

# Root-cause remediation
A defect is not closed when its symptom is gone.
Two more things are owed: the cause, and the **process** that let the cause reach a user or an expensive gate.
## When this applies
Either of:
- the defect **reached a released version**; or
- the defect **turned a PR red on a check that a cheaper detector could have run.**
The second trigger is a question, not a stopwatch: what separates is whether the same failure was reachable earlier and more cheaply than the gate that found it.
Answer it by naming the cheaper detector and its standing cost, or by recording that none exists.
A worked example of each:
- **Qualifies.** `closure.py no-copies` refused a test symbol that shared a name with a production symbol, after roughly fifteen minutes of CI.
The same check runs locally in **under a second** and existed already — it was simply in no local path.
Cheaper detector: an edit-time hook; built — sooner, not a repair, and no autofix.
- **Does not qualify.** A solver regression caught by the golden fixtures.
The cheapest detector that would have caught it *is* the gate that caught it.
Record the finding, build nothing.
## What is owed
**Fix the defect** under normal policy (`fixer.md`); nothing here replaces it.
**In parallel, and in a separate seat**, establish the root cause and the **process root cause**.
A separate seat because the fixer is invested in the fix; independence here is procedural, exactly as it is for `fix-review`.
**Address the root cause.** Countermeasures include worker instructions, the plan, testing procedure, a local check, a hook, a CI change.
When the defect was found late in CI, a cheaper and earlier detector is strongly preferred.
**Address the process root cause when it pays for itself** — see the cost test below.
**A countermeasure is a change like any other**: reproduced, verified, mutation-proven, independently reviewed.
## The process root cause
Every process failure is in exactly one of four states:
- **(a) The process did not exist.**
- **(b) The process existed and was not followed.**
- **(c) The process was followed and did not produce the intended result.**
- **(d) The process was sound and its preconditions changed underneath it.**
Name the state.
The countermeasure differs by state, and the most common mistake is treating (c) or (d) as (b) — writing a firmer instruction when the instruction was obeyed and wrong.
A check half-ported out of its lane is **(c)**: #2073's step 6d ran and passed on every stale-pin PR while its unit read one of `mutation`'s two directions.
For **(d)**, the countermeasure is rarely a new rule: it is making the process notice its own precondition change.
Permanent countermeasures may change how plans, rosters and briefs are made; how worker instructions are written; or repository conventions and policy.
**Repository rules and policy are changed only with the owner's approval**, and the request states which of the four states it addresses.
## The cost test
Implement a countermeasure when
cost(countermeasure, recurring) < cost(defect) x P(recurrence)
Both sides in the same unit: **wall-clock, per occurrence, over a release cycle**.
State the numbers, do not assert the conclusion.
- `cost(countermeasure, recurring)` is the standing cost — the seconds it adds to every run, every session, forever — not the once-off cost of writing it.
- `P(recurrence)` uses the **measured class frequency** where one exists; otherwise state the estimate and its basis.
**"No countermeasure" is a legitimate, recordable outcome.** Some defects are irreducible: the cheapest detector that would have caught them is the gate that did.

A check that passes while the bug is present is worse than no check: it converts an open defect into a closed one.

The shape keeps recurring here — a key-set check that supplied the value it asserted, an invariant green on a broken tree, an autofix successful while skipping its own repair — each caught by a contro
A check over a structured input is registered in `field_coverage.mjs`: a governance check is in the derived set and registers its input or declares none.

**A finding that changes how a later stage must work is written into that stage's own brief by the time the PR that produced it merges.**

The finding must be **established by measurement with its null control** — the perturbation that would have made it fail — not by argument.
An unverified observation is not carried; it is measured first or dropped.
Given that, it applies whenever the finding does any of three things to a stage that has not started:
- **narrows what that stage may do** — a technique it was expected to use is refused, or is now legitimate only under a precondition;
- **invalidates an assumption it rests on** — a figure, a partition, an environment, a tool version it was scored against turns out not to hold;
- **removes an option it was expected to have** — a dependency will not install, a budget it was to spend has been spent, an interface is not available.

On **pull requests only**, the gate runs just the scripts the change can reach:

### The gate lock on a shared box
`tests/stress.py` measures this machine while it solves, so only one agent on a box may run it at a time.
`run.sh` takes the lease for each `stress.py` run alone and releases it after; every other script runs unleased.
By hand, to measure across commands, use `tests/gate_lock.py` — not `mkdir /tmp/hpo-gate.lock` and a shell pid:

```bash python3 tests/gate_lock.py take --label <your-label> python3 tests/gate_lock.py renew --label <your-label> # between commands python3 tests/gate_lock.py release --label <your-label> python3 te
The owner file at `/tmp/hpo-gate.lock/owner` carries your label and an `expires_at` lease (30 minutes, above the longest observed stress run).
Waiters queue by priority band, then arrival (`ticket-<n>`; a dead or expired ticket is skipped), and `renew` exits 75 while one waits.
An expired lease, or an abandoned hold (`holding` marker, no live flock), may be taken without forensics.
Whoever runs `stress.py` under the lease holds `flock` on `/tmp/hpo-gate.lock/flock`, so a crash drops it and the next waiter takes at once (#404).

A test may build inputs and expected *values*.
